etymology: Hebrew Azeqah, perhaps “tilled” or “dug over,” a fortified town in the lowland of Judah.
biblical_def: Azekah was a fenced city in the Shephelah, the lowland of Judah, set on the road that descended from the hill country toward the Philistine plain. It was unto Azekah that the LORD chased the five Amorite kings in the great battle for Gibeon, casting down upon them the great hailstones from heaven, so that more died of the hail than of the sword (Josh 10:11). The town was reckoned among the cities of Judah’s lowland (Josh 15:35) and was fortified by Rehoboam among the defences of the kingdom (2Ch 11:9). It was between Shochoh and Azekah, at Ephes-dammim, that the Philistines pitched their camp when Goliath defied the armies of the living God and David slew him with a sling and a stone (1Sa 17:1). In the last days of Judah, when Nebuchadnezzar’s army was sweeping the land, Azekah and Lachish were the only fenced cities that remained, and the prophet Jeremiah names them as the last to fall (Jer 34:7). Azekah thus stands at the beginning and the ending of Judah’s story in the land: a witness to the LORD’s deliverance by hailstones and by a shepherd’s sling, and a witness to the judgment that at last overtook a people who would not return to their God.
webster_summary: A fortified town in the lowland of Judah, near the field of David and Goliath; one of the last cities to fall to Babylon.

With Lachish it was among the last fenced cities to fall to Babylon (Jer 34:7).

corruption_summary: A place-name, not a doctrine in dispute; its lesson spans God’s deliverance and His judgment upon an impenitent people.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the same God who delivered Israel at Azekah by hailstones, and gave the giant into David’s hand near its walls, also gave Azekah up to Babylon when Judah would not repent. The Lord who saves is the Lord who judges; His patience is long, but His justice is sure, and a people who spurn His mercy will at last meet His rod.

Azekah at the field of Ephes-dammim also enshrines the lesson of David and Goliath: the battle is the LORD’s, and He saves not with sword and spear. The youth who came in the name of the LORD of hosts overthrew the champion of the Philistines, that all the earth might know there is a God in Israel. Faith in the living God, not the arm of flesh, is the strength of His people.

etymology: Hebrew Qiryath-sepher, “city of the book” or “town of the scribe,” the older name of Debir in the hill country of Judah.
biblical_def: Kirjath-sepher, “the city of the book,” was the former name of Debir, a town in the hill country of Judah (Josh 15:15). When Caleb came to drive out the sons of Anak and take possession of his inheritance, he made a promise: “He that smiteth Kirjathsepher, and taketh it, to him will I give Achsah my daughter to wife” (Josh 15:16). Othniel the son of Kenaz, Caleb’s younger brother, took the city, and won Achsah for his bride; and the same Othniel afterward became the first of the judges, on whom the Spirit of the LORD came to deliver Israel (Judg 3:9–10). Achsah, asking her father for a field, prayed also for springs of water, and Caleb gave her the upper and the nether springs (Josh 15:19). The town was later given to the priests as one of their cities (Josh 21:15). The name “city of the book” has stirred much wonder, suggesting a place of writing or record among the Canaanites. Whatever learning the old city held, it could not save it from the hand of the LORD’s people; and the man who took it rose to be the first deliverer of Israel. Kirjath-sepher witnesses that valour rewarded in faith opens the way to greater service in the kingdom of God.
webster_summary: The old name of Debir, “city of the book,” taken by Othniel, who won Caleb’s daughter and became Israel’s first judge.

corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the path from Kirjath-sepher to the seat of the judge. Othniel proved himself in the taking of the city, and the man who was faithful in that smaller charge was raised up by the Spirit of God to deliver all Israel. The Lord trains His servants for great work by their faithfulness in lesser tasks.

The “city of the book,” whatever its learning, fell before the people of God; and it is worth remembering that the only book that abides is the book of the LORD. The records and wisdom of the nations pass away with their cities, but the word of our God shall stand for ever. Achsah’s request for the springs of water also teaches the boldness of faith that asks for the fuller blessing and is not denied.

etymology: Hebrew Gibbethon, “a height” or “a mound,” a Philistine town in the lot of Dan, given to the Levites.
biblical_def: Gibbethon was a town on the Philistine border, assigned to the tribe of Dan and given to the Levites of the Kohathite family (Josh 19:44; 21:23), but held by the Philistines through much of Israel’s history. Its siege became the scene of two royal assassinations in the northern kingdom. While Nadab the son of Jeroboam, with all Israel, laid siege to Gibbethon, Baasha conspired against him and slew him there, then reigned in his stead and destroyed all the house of Jeroboam (1Ki 15:27). A generation later, Israel was again encamped against Gibbethon when word came that Zimri had murdered Elah the son of Baasha; the army in the field made Omri their captain king, and he went up from Gibbethon to besiege Zimri in Tirzah (1Ki 16:15–17). Thus the same Philistine stronghold witnessed the fall of two dynasties of Israel, the houses of Jeroboam and of Baasha alike cut off in fulfillment of the word of the LORD. Gibbethon, a town Israel could never firmly hold, became instead the ground where the LORD’s judgments upon the apostate northern kings were set in motion. It is a sober monument to the truth that thrones built upon idolatry and bloodshed do not stand.
webster_summary: A Philistine-held Levitical town in Dan, twice besieged by Israel; scene of the falls of the houses of Jeroboam and Baasha.

corruption_summary: A place-name, not a doctrine in dispute; its lesson is that thrones built on idolatry and blood do not stand.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the LORD’s faithfulness to His threatenings. He had decreed the cutting off of Jeroboam’s house for its idolatry, and of Baasha’s house after it; and at Gibbethon, far from the throne-city, His word came to pass. The judgments of God upon sin are not idle words; they ripen in their season and fall with certainty.

Gibbethon also displays the unrest of the northern kingdom, where king murdered king and dynasty devoured dynasty. A kingdom founded in rebellion against the house of David and in the worship of golden calves knew no settled peace. Sin breeds disorder; the throne that despises God’s appointed order reaps treason and bloodshed in its own house.

etymology: Hebrew Gederah, “a sheepfold” or “an enclosure,” from gader, a wall or hedge; a town in the lowland of Judah.
biblical_def: Gederah was a town in the Shephelah, the lowland of Judah, named among the cities of that region in the inheritance of the tribe (Josh 15:36). Its name means “a sheepfold” or “an enclosure,” from the Hebrew word for a wall or hedge, and it belonged to a family of place-names — Geder, Gederah, Gederoth, Gederothaim — all marking walled or hedged settlements among the fields. The Chronicles preserve a glimpse of the humble life of such a town: among the descendants of Judah were “the potters, and those that dwelt among plants and hedges: there they dwelt with the king for his work” (1Ch 4:23), craftsmen who served the crown in their quiet labour. From Gederah came Jozabad the Gederathite, one of the mighty men who joined themselves to David at Ziklag (1Ch 12:4). Though Gederah is little mentioned, it stands for the many ordinary towns of Judah whose people tended sheep, worked the potter’s wheel, and served their king in obscurity. It witnesses that the kingdom of God is upheld not only by the famous but by the faithful labour of countless hidden hands, whose names are known to the LORD though forgotten by men.
webster_summary: A town in the lowland of Judah whose name means “sheepfold”; home of one of David’s mighty men.

corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the dignity of obscure and faithful work. The potters and herdsmen of Gederah dwelt with the king for his work, serving the crown in their quiet craft. The kingdom of God, like the kingdom of Judah, is upheld by the unnoticed labour of many hands, and the LORD honours such service though the world forgets it.

Gederah, the “sheepfold,” also calls to mind the flock of God gathered within His enclosure. As the shepherd folds his sheep behind the wall for safety, so the Lord gathers His people into the fold of the church, where they are kept by His care. The lowly name of a Judean town becomes a quiet emblem of the safety of the flock under the Good Shepherd.

etymology: Hebrew Beth-Dagon, “house of Dagon,” a town named for the Philistine fish-god, in the lowland of Judah.
biblical_def: Beth-dagon, “the house of Dagon,” was a town in the lowland of Judah toward the Philistine border (Josh 15:41); another town of the same name lay in the lot of Asher (Josh 19:27). The name preserves the worship of Dagon, the chief idol of the Philistines, whose temples stood at Ashdod and Gaza. Dagon is forever bound up in Scripture with his own humiliation before the ark of the LORD: when the Philistines set the captured ark in the house of Dagon at Ashdod, they found their god fallen on his face before it; and when they set him up again, the next morning the head of Dagon and both the palms of his hands were cut off upon the threshold, and only the stump was left (1Sa 5:4). So the dead idol bowed before the living God. That a town in Judah bore the name “house of Dagon” testifies to how deeply Canaanite and Philistine idolatry had marked the land before Israel possessed it, and how the names of false gods clung to places long after. Beth-dagon stands as a silent witness against idolatry, recalling the day the LORD broke the idol upon his own threshold and proved that there is no god beside Him.
webster_summary: A town named “house of Dagon” for the Philistine idol; a reminder of the god the LORD broke before His ark.

corruption_summary: A place-name preserving an idol’s name; its lesson is the impotence of false gods before the living LORD.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the idol Dagon, whose name clung to the town, was shown to be nothing before the ark of the LORD. The dead image fell on its face and was broken upon its own threshold; the gods of the heathen cannot stand in the presence of the God of Israel. Every Beth-dagon in the land was a monument to a god the LORD had already proved powerless.

Beth-dagon also testifies how thoroughly idolatry had saturated the land before Israel came, so that towns bore the names of false gods. The believer is warned how easily the worship of the world leaves its mark upon places and peoples; yet the gospel breaks the idols of every Beth-dagon, as the ark broke Dagon, and sets the living God in the place where dead images once stood.

etymology: Hebrew Ma’on, “a dwelling” or “habitation,” a town in the hill country of Judah with a wilderness about it.
biblical_def: Maon was a town in the hill country of Judah (Josh 15:55), set on the edge of a wilderness that bore its name, in the dry pasture-land south of Hebron. It was in the wilderness of Maon that David hid from Saul, and there Saul nearly took him: David was on one side of the mountain and Saul on the other, and Saul had compassed David and his men round about, when a messenger came that the Philistines had invaded the land, and Saul was forced to turn away — so that the place was called the rock of divisions (1Sa 23:24–28). In Maon also dwelt Nabal, a man very great in flocks but churlish and evil in his doings, whose possessions were in nearby Carmel (1Sa 25:2). When Nabal returned David’s kindness with insult, David purposed vengeance, but the wise and gracious Abigail met him with her gift and her counsel, and turned away his wrath; and the LORD Himself smote Nabal that he died (1Sa 25). Maon thus stands as a place of David’s testing in the wilderness years, where the LORD delivered him from Saul by a sudden providence and kept him from avenging himself by the timely wisdom of a godly woman. It witnesses the watchful care of God over His anointed in the days of his affliction.
webster_summary: A town in the hill country of Judah with a wilderness about it, where David hid from Saul and Nabal dwelt.

corruption_summary: A place-name, not a doctrine in dispute; its lesson is the watchful providence of God over His servant in affliction.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the providence that twice delivered David at Maon. When Saul had all but closed his net, a Philistine raid drew him away at the very hour of David’s peril; and when David himself was about to sin in vengeance against Nabal, God sent Abigail to stay his hand. The LORD watches over His own, delivering them both from their enemies and from their own rash anger.

Maon also sets the churlish Nabal beside the prudent Abigail, the fool who despised David against the wise woman who honoured the LORD’s anointed. Nabal’s name means “fool,” and his end proved it; vengeance belonged to God, who smote him without David lifting a hand. The believer learns at Maon to leave his cause with the Lord rather than avenge himself.

etymology: Hebrew Ayyalon, “place of deer” or “field of stags,” from a word for the hart.
biblical_def: Aijalon was a town and the broad valley below the pass of Beth-horon, lying on the western edge of the hill country where it opens toward the plain. The valley of Aijalon is forever joined to the day of Joshua’s long battle, for when he pursued the Amorite kings he cried, “Sun, stand thou still upon Gibeon; and thou, Moon, in the valley of Ajalon” (Josh 10:12), and the sun stood still and the moon stayed until the people had avenged themselves upon their enemies. The town was given to the tribe of Dan and assigned to the Levites, the sons of Kohath (Josh 21:24), yet the Danites could not at first drive out the Amorites who dwelt there (Judg 1:35). Aijalon was later fortified by Rehoboam among the defences of Judah (2Ch 11:10), and in Ahaz’s evil reign the Philistines seized it (2Ch 28:18). Standing at the meeting of highland and lowland, the valley of Aijalon was a frequent road of war; but Scripture remembers it above all as the place over which the moon stayed at the word of the LORD, a witness that the heavens obey the God of Israel.
webster_summary: A town and valley on the western slopes of the hill country, where the moon stayed at Joshua’s command.

corruption_summary: A place-name, not a doctrine in dispute; its lesson is that the heavens obey the command of the LORD.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the plain testimony of Joshua 10: at the word of God, spoken through His servant, the sun and moon stayed their course until the victory was complete. The dictionary receives the long day as the inspired record gives it — a real act of the God who made and rules the lights of heaven.

The valley of Aijalon thus stands against every attempt to reduce the miracle to a poetic figure or a later legend. The text appeals to the book of Jasher as a known witness and declares plainly that “there was no day like that before it or after it” (Josh 10:14). What God has done, He has done; the believer’s part is to wonder and adore.
roots_summary: The name comes from a Hebrew word for the deer or hart, marking the valley as a haunt of game.

etymology: Hebrew Be’eroth, “wells” or “cisterns,” the plural of be’er, a well; a Gibeonite town reckoned to Benjamin.
biblical_def: Beeroth, “the wells,” was one of the four cities of the Gibeonites who deceived Joshua into a league of peace by their pretended journey, and so escaped the destruction appointed for the Canaanites (Josh 9:17). It was afterward reckoned to the tribe of Benjamin (Josh 18:25). From Beeroth came Rechab and Baanah, the two captains of bands who treacherously murdered Ish-bosheth the son of Saul as he lay upon his bed at noon, and brought his head to David at Hebron, thinking to win reward; but David, abhorring the deed, commanded that they be slain for shedding the blood of a righteous man in his own house (2Sa 4:2–12). Beeroth was also the home of Naharai, the armourbearer of Joab, who is numbered among David’s mighty men (2Sa 23:37). After the captivity the men of Beeroth returned to dwell again in their town (Ezra 2:25). The name fittingly recalls the wells of water that made the place a settlement; but its story in Scripture is chiefly the story of treachery rightly punished, for David would not let the murder of Saul’s son go unavenged, even when it seemed to serve his own advantage. Beeroth witnesses that the throne of the righteous is established by justice and not by the shedding of innocent blood.
webster_summary: A Gibeonite town reckoned to Benjamin; home of the murderers of Ish-bosheth, whom David justly slew.

scriptures: And the children of Israel journeyed, and came unto their cities on the third day. Now their cities were Gibeon, and Chephirah, and Beeroth, and Kirjathjearim.

And Saul's son had two men that were captains of bands: the name of the one was Baanah, and the name of the other Rechab, the sons of Rimmon a Beerothite, of the children of Benjamin: (for Beeroth also was reckoned to Benjamin:

And David commanded his young men, and they slew them, and cut off their hands and their feet, and hanged them up over the pool in Hebron. But they took the head of Ishbosheth, and buried it in the sepulchre of Abner in Hebron.
corruption_summary: A place-name, not a doctrine in dispute; its lesson is that the righteous throne is established by justice, not by innocent blood.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is David’s refusal to profit by murder. The men of Beeroth thought to please the king by slaying his rival; but David, who would not lift his hand against Saul, abhorred the shedding of Ish-bosheth’s blood and avenged it. The kingdom of the righteous is not built upon treachery; the end does not sanctify the murder.

Beeroth, the town of wells, also recalls the league of Gibeon, by which a people spared through deceit yet became hewers of wood and drawers of water for the house of God. The LORD honoured even the oath sworn to the Gibeonites, and later punished Saul’s house for breaking it (2Sa 21). God keeps His covenants and requires that men keep theirs; the oath of the LORD is not to be lightly broken.
roots_summary: The name is the plural of be’er, “a well,” marking a settlement of wells or cisterns.
roots_lines: Beeroth — Hebrew Be’eroth, “wells” or “cisterns.”
It is the plural of be’er, a well of water.
It was one of the four Gibeonite cities.
It was reckoned to the tribe of Benjamin.
The town of wells became known for treachery justly avenged.
usage: Like David at Beeroth, the righteous will not build a throne upon the shedding of innocent blood.
Beeroth teaches that the LORD keeps His covenants and requires men to keep their oaths.
The murderers of Beeroth found that treachery in a good cause is still murder before God.

etymology: Hebrew Kephirah, “a young lion” or “a village,” one of the Gibeonite towns in Benjamin.
biblical_def: Chephirah was one of the four cities of the Gibeonites who, hearing what Joshua had done to Jericho and Ai, came with worn shoes and mouldy bread, feigning to be travellers from a far country, and so obtained a league of peace from the princes of Israel (Josh 9:17). When the deceit was discovered, Joshua would not break the oath sworn in the name of the LORD, but made the Gibeonites hewers of wood and drawers of water for the congregation and for the altar of God (Josh 9:21). Chephirah fell within the inheritance of Benjamin, named among the cities of that tribe (Josh 18:26), and after the Babylonian captivity its men returned with the remnant to dwell again in the land (Ezra 2:25; Neh 7:29). Little else is recorded of the town. Yet Chephirah, with Gibeon, Beeroth, and Kirjath-jearim, bears witness to a striking truth: that the LORD honoured the oath made even to a people who had won it by deceit, and would not let it be broken. When Saul long afterward slew the Gibeonites in his zeal, the LORD sent famine upon Israel until the wrong was righted (2Sa 21:1). Chephirah thus stands within the story of God’s jealous regard for the sanctity of a sworn covenant.
webster_summary: One of the four Gibeonite cities, reckoned to Benjamin; a witness to the sanctity of a sworn oath.
webster_full: CHEPHIRAH, one of the four cities of the Gibeonites (Josh 9:17).
Its people gained a league of peace from Joshua by deceit.
It fell within the inheritance of Benjamin (Josh 18:26).
Its men returned from the captivity to dwell there again (Ezra 2:25).
Its name signifies a young lion or, by another sense, a village.
scriptures: And the children of Israel journeyed, and came unto their cities on the third day. Now their cities were Gibeon, and Chephirah, and Beeroth, and Kirjathjearim.
And Mizpeh, and Chephirah, and Mozah,
The children of Kirjatharim, Chephirah, and Beeroth, seven hundred and forty and three.
And the princes said unto them, Let them live; but let them be hewers of wood and drawers of water unto all the congregation; as the princes had promised them.
corruption_summary: A place-name, not a doctrine in dispute; its lesson is the LORD’s jealous regard for the sanctity of a sworn covenant.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the binding force of an oath sworn in the name of the LORD. Though the Gibeonites of Chephirah won their league by deceit, Israel had sworn, and the oath stood; Joshua would not break it, and God Himself avenged it when Saul did. The modern age treats vows lightly, but the LORD holds men to the words of their mouth.

Chephirah and its sister-towns also show mercy mingled with judgment. The Gibeonites were spared, but made servants of the sanctuary, hewing wood and drawing water for the altar. Their cunning brought them into bondage, yet a bondage in the service of the house of God — better far than the destruction that fell on the other Canaanites. So the LORD often turns even the crooked devices of men to a place near His worship.
roots_summary: The name means “a young lion,” or by another reading “a village,” borne by a Gibeonite town.
roots_lines: Chephirah — Hebrew Kephirah, “a young lion” or “a village.”

Its men are numbered among those returned from Babylon.
The lion-named town witnesses the binding force of a sworn oath.
usage: Like Israel toward Chephirah, the people of God keep an oath sworn in His name, though it cost them.
Chephirah teaches that the LORD holds men to their vows and avenges broken covenants.
The servitude of the Gibeonites shows mercy mingled with judgment near the house of God.

etymology: Hebrew Rechob, “a broad place” or “open street,” a town in the lot of Asher.
biblical_def: Rehob was a town in the inheritance of the tribe of Asher, in the north of the land toward Zidon and the entering in of Hamath (Josh 19:28, 30). Like Jokneam and the towns of Zebulun, it was set apart with its suburbs to the Levites of the family of Gershon (Josh 21:31). Yet Rehob belongs also to the sorrowful catalogue of the first chapter of Judges, for Asher failed to drive out its Canaanite inhabitants: “Neither did Asher drive out the inhabitants of Accho, nor the inhabitants of Zidon, nor of Ahlab, nor of Achzib, nor of Helbah, nor of Aphik, nor of Rehob” (Judg 1:31). The Asherites dwelt among the Canaanites rather than dispossessing them, and so the unconquered town remained. The name Rehob, “a broad place,” is the same word used for the open street or square of a city. There was another Beth-rehob far to the north, near the approach to Hamath, which gave its name to a small Syrian kingdom (2Sa 10:6). The Asherite Rehob takes its place among the towns that mark Israel’s incomplete obedience — a Levitical city that should have been wholly the LORD’s, left half in the hands of the heathen. It witnesses that even the towns given to God’s ministers were not exempt from the cost of a faith that failed to finish.
webster_summary: A Levitical town in Asher’s lot whose Canaanites were never driven out; its name means “a broad place.”
webster_full: REHOB, a town in the inheritance of Asher, toward Zidon and Hamath.
It was given with its suburbs to the Levites of Gershon (Josh 21:31).

Its name signifies a broad place or open street.

corruption_summary: A place-name, not a doctrine in dispute; its lesson is that even towns given to God’s ministers suffered the cost of unfinished obedience.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that Rehob, set apart for the Levites, was yet left half in Canaanite hands because Asher would not finish the work. A town meant wholly for the LORD’s service became a place of compromise. The lesson is solemn: even what is dedicated to God may be defiled when His people lack the resolve to drive out what He commanded them to remove.

Rehob, “the broad place,” also bears a quiet irony. Its name speaks of openness and room, yet Israel’s failure there narrowed the inheritance God had given. The broad place that should have been wholly the LORD’s was crowded with the idols of the heathen. So a soul made for the wide liberty of God’s service is cramped and straitened when it makes room for the world alongside the worship of the LORD.
roots_summary: The name means “a broad place” or “open street,” the same word used for a city’s square.

usage: Like Asher at Rehob, God’s people may leave even a dedicated place half in the hands of the heathen.
Rehob teaches that the broad liberty of God’s service is straitened when room is made for the world.
Even a Levitical town suffered the cost of a faith that failed to finish the work.
